intro: Local governments here pay interest on their bonds. This page lists the amounts, the money they hold on deposit, and what other places have done with shared funds.

leaving.title: Interest on local bonds
leaving.lead: Interest is the price of borrowing. These are the amounts in local governments’ own bond papers.

grow_lead: Arkansas law keeps county and city money out of the stock market (only safe securities of five years or less). This section lists examples of shared funds elsewhere.

levers.title: Paying down debt faster
levers.body: The interest paid on a bond depends on the interest rate and the number of years the money is borrowed.

precedents.name: Alaska Permanent Fund
precedents.fact: By law, Alaska may draw only 5% a year of the fund’s average value; the rest keeps growing. That draw now supplies over half of the state’s unrestricted general-fund revenue, plus a yearly dividend to residents ($1,000 in 2025).

levers.here: The Arkadelphia School District’s new high school bonds borrow $37.17 million and repay $74.54 million over 30 years (2026 Official Statement, p. 12). In the model on the What-if page, the same bonds at the same rate, paid with the full debt tax, would be paid off in about 7 years with about $6.8 million of interest (modeled; the assumptions are on that page).
levers.limit: Saving first means waiting for the building, and the full debt tax isn’t free until the older bonds are paid.

levers.title: Revolving loan funds
levers.body: A revolving fund lends to projects and takes the repayments, with interest, back into the same fund.

precedents.name: State revolving funds for water
precedents.fact: Water and sewer loans are repaid with interest into the same fund, which lends it out again. Federal seed money of about $21 billion has turned into more than $41 billion of help this way (through 2019).

precedents.name: Bank of North Dakota
precedents.fact: Opened July 28, 1919 — the only state-owned bank in the nation. State money is deposited with it and lent back into the state.

levers.limit: A revolving fund only works if loans get repaid; a fund that forgives its own loans shrinks.

levers.title: Community-owned utilities, co-ops, and land trusts
levers.body: Some communities own utilities, co-ops, and land trusts. The examples below come from public records.

precedents.name: Rural electric co-ops
precedents.fact: Private power companies wouldn’t wire farms — too few customers per mile. Neighbors formed nonprofit co-ops, and the 1936 Rural Electrification Act lent them the money to build.

precedents.name: Margins go back to members
precedents.fact: A co-op returns what it doesn’t need as “capital credits.” Since 1990, electric co-ops have returned nearly $13 billion to their members.

precedents.name: Arkansas’s co-ops
precedents.fact: Arkansas’s electric co-ops cover more than 60% of the state’s land and serve more than 1 million members, through 17 member-owned local co-ops.

precedents.name: One here already
precedents.fact: South Central Arkansas Electric Cooperative is headquartered in Arkadelphia. It was organized July 31, 1940, and serves parts of eight counties west and southwest of town.

precedents.name: Conway Corporation
precedents.fact: The City of Conway’s own not-for-profit utility company, incorporated in 1929 — electric, water, and cable and internet — with no profit motive, in its CEO’s words.

precedents.name: Paragould Light, Water & Cable
precedents.fact: Paragould’s city-owned utility: electric since 1938, water and wastewater added in 1984, cable in 1989.

precedents.name: Chattanooga’s EPB
precedents.fact: The city’s own electric utility launched the first community-wide gigabit fiber network in the U.S. in 2010. A 2025 University of Tennessee at Chattanooga study, conducted by Bento Lobo of the UTC Rollins College of Business, estimated the economic impact of EPB’s fiber network and smart grid at $5.3 billion since launch.

precedents.name: Champlain Housing Trust
precedents.fact: Founded in 1984 with the City of Burlington, Vermont’s support, to keep homes permanently affordable — the land stays in the trust, so each home stays affordable for the next family.

levers.limit: Owning things means running them well: a utility or land trust needs good management, reserves for repairs, and customers who stay.

guardrails.lead: Elinor Ostrom won the 2009 Nobel Prize in economics “for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons.” She studied shared resources that people ran well for generations, and found eight things they had in common:
principles: Clear boundaries — who the fund belongs to, and what it’s for.
Rules that fit this place — written for local needs, not copied.
The people affected help make the rules.
Someone accountable checks — in the open.
Penalties start small and grow for repeat misuse.
Cheap, local ways to settle disputes.
Outside authorities respect the community’s right to run it.
For big shared resources, layers — local groups inside larger ones.
guardrails.warning: In 1994, Orange County, California’s treasurer borrowed against the county’s $7.6 billion investment pool to chase higher returns. It lost about $1.7 billion and the county filed for bankruptcy.

law.text: Arkansas counties and cities may invest spare money only in safe securities of five years or less, bank deposits, and similar — not stocks.
A new or higher local sales tax — including one dedicated to a fund — needs a vote of the people.
Arkansas’s Interlocal Cooperation Act lets local governments work together on shared services. Exactly how far it lets them lend to each other is an open question we’re checking.

residents: Outcomes are tracked on What came of it; public meetings are on the calendar.
Residents have started petitions on ideas like this — see petitions.
limits: Shared funds can be mismanaged, raided, or spent on the wrong things. The safeguards above exist because that happens.
A dollar saved is a dollar not spent on something people need now. Every choice here is a trade.
Examples from other places show what’s possible, not what will work here. Each took years, local leaders, and often state or federal help.
None of this is a recommendation. It is a map of options, with the record of each.
